extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for handling confidential/trade secret materials, motions for protective orders, discovery limits, depositions, filing/redaction procedures, and pretrial/telephone conferences in TTAB (Trademark Trial and Appeal Board) proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑use/disclosure restriction under protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: A party will not disclose or make use of confidential or trade secret information provided to it under the order except for purposes of the proceeding in which the information is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective orders limit use/disclosure to the proceeding; parties bound by order must not use confidential materials outside that scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means for resolving confidentiality disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The means for resolving disputes over whether particular matter constitutes confidential or trade secret information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective orders should include dispute-resolution procedures for disagreements about confidentiality designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing confidential materials procedure (ESTTA/paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential or trade secret material shall be submitted to the Board electronically designated as 'CONFIDENTIAL' in ESTTA, or by paper in a separate sealed envelope or other sealed container bearing the proceeding number and name and an indication of the general nature of the contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For confidential submissions filed either via ESTTA or by paper, two versions are required – a confidential version as well as a redacted version available for public viewing. Electronic filing via ESTTA is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return or destruction at termination
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of the proceeding, each party shall return to the disclosing party all confidential information and materials, including all copies, summaries, and abstracts thereof, or the disclosing party may request destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within 30 days after final termination parties/attorneys must return protected information or request destruction. Because the Board's jurisdiction ends at termination, parties often stipulate to a protective order to create contract rights enforceable in court post-termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's jurisdiction and archival retention
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's jurisdiction over the parties and their attorneys ends when the proceeding is terminated; parties may agree that archival copies may be retained subject to agreed safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board cannot supervise materials after termination; parties should use stipulated orders to bind them post-termination where desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redaction standard: rule of reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing protected information or a brief that discusses such information, the protected information or portion should be redacted from the remainder. A rule of reasonableness should dictate how redaction is effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a short portion of a page is confidential, cover that portion; if most of a page is confidential, file the whole page under seal. When most pages contain confidential material, submitting the entire document under seal may be reasonable. Whole-document filings under seal should be very rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking and labeling sealed submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Protected information and pleadings/briefs that reproduce or discuss such information shall be filed under seal; the envelope/container shall be prominently stamped 'CONFIDENTIAL' and identify the proceeding and nature of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested legend: 'FILED UNDER SEAL SUBJECT TO PROTECTIVE ORDER.' Include proceeding number, parties, and a description of the contents (e.g., 'Applicant's Answers to Opposer's Interrogatories 8 and 19').

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to designate confidential at time of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: To be handled as confidential pursuant to the Board’s standard protective order or an individualized order, confidential materials must be so designated at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper or electronic submissions not properly designated as confidential will be placed in the public records (TTABVUE). Failure to provide a redacted version may result in waiver of confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESTTA confidential filing mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: When using ESTTA for confidential filings, the filer should select 'CONFIDENTIAL Opposition, Cancellation or Concurrent Use' under 'File Documents in a Board Proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filings made using this option will not be available for public viewing; entries will appear on the public docket sheet indicating receipt. Confidential materials may be inspected only by those authorized under the protective order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board handling and storage of confidential materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential materials submitted via ESTTA will not be made available for public viewing; confidential paper filings under seal are stored in a secure location and disclosed only to the Board and those specified in the protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential material is given full consideration in rulings but will not be disclosed in orders/decisions. After final determination the Board will contact parties to arrange return/retrieval or require consent to disposal; absent response, materials may be destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR/TTAB rules on confidentiality (37 CFR §2.27/§2.126)
rubrics_metrics.description: Files are generally public after registration or publication; anything ordered to be filed under seal pursuant to protective order shall be kept confidential and not made available unless ordered otherwise. Submissions handled as confidential must be under separate cover and a redacted copy submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR §2.27(d)-(e) and §2.126(c); limited handling requirements and redaction obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of protective relief available (per FRCP 26(c)/37 CFR §2.120(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: For good cause, the Board may make any order which justice requires to protect a party from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue burden or expense, including: forbidding disclosure; specifying terms for disclosure; prescribing discovery methods; limiting scope; designating who may be present; sealing depositions; protecting trade secrets; requiring simultaneous sealed filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may adopt one or more of the orders analogous to Rule 26(c)(1) relief as justice requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause standard for protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must establish good cause to obtain a protective order by providing 'a particular and specific demonstration of fact, as distinguished from stereotyped and conclusory statements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cause is a factual determination based on nature/character of requested information weighed against issues in the proceeding; movant bears the burden and must show prejudice to ability to litigate, not merely increased difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's options when granting protective motion
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board grants a motion for protective order it may direct the parties to prepare a mutually agreeable order, approve a proffered order, order parties to adhere to the Board’s standard protective order, or provide other appropriate relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties often negotiate terms in good faith; the Board can adopt or require a specific form of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to confer before seeking protective relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties should confer in good faith before seeking Board intervention for a protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certification of conferral is a requirement in analogous federal rules; the Board expects parties to attempt resolution before motion practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary standard for prohibiting depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuance of a protective order totally prohibiting a deposition occurs only in extraordinary circumstances; the Board may limit or order that a deposition not be had if discovery is obtainable from other sources that are more convenient, less burdensome, or duplicative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movant bears the burden to show good cause with specific facts; lack of personal knowledge alone is insufficient absent showing of other available sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique/ superior knowledge test for high‑level officials
rubrics_metrics.description: To prohibit a deposition of a very high‑level official, the movant must demonstrate that the official has no direct knowledge of relevant facts or that other persons have equal or greater knowledge; if movant meets this initial burden, burden shifts to the party seeking the deposition to show unique/superior knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the seeking party fails to show unique knowledge, Board will grant protection and require less intrusive discovery (deposit of lower‑level employees, 30(b)(6), interrogatories, requests for production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits based on number/timing/duplication of depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may move for protection if a notice of deposition would exceed the permitted number of ten discovery depositions, result in a second deposition of an individual, or be outside the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling and numeric limits are relevant to motions for protective orders; mere busyness of deponent is generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for vacating/ modifying protective order to allow deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to vacate or modify a protective order should include (1) a reasonable indication that the deposition may lead to admissible evidence, and (2) that less intrusive methods are unsatisfactory, insufficient or inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If granted, Board may limit topics and duration; examples show Board has limited depositions to specific hours or topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical or health‑based deposition protections
rubrics_metrics.description: A party moving for a protective order to delay, limit or prevent a deposition on the basis of medical grounds or health concerns has the burden of making a specific and documented factual showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General assertions of health concerns are insufficient; documentary evidence required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper use of protective order as discovery response
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where discovery requests are so oppressive as to constitute clear harassment, it is generally improper to respond to a request for discovery by filing a motion for protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy for excessive interrogatories is service of a general objection rather than a protective order; motions for protective orders should not be used to delay or harass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board determination of need for protection on particular requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must determine whether protection is needed against a particular interrogatory or request for production/admission due to their nature or whether the volume renders them harassing and oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether requests are tailored to issues in the proceeding and consider proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider proportionality and to confer
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are expected to take into account principles of proportionality with regard to document requests and requests for admission and to confer in good faith about the proper scope of discovery pursuant to 37 CFR §2.120(a) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation and conferral minimize need for motions; scope should be tailored to issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone conferences for discovery motions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a stipulation or motion in an inter partes proceeding is such that resolution by correspondence is impractical, the Board may address the matter by telephone conference involving the parties and a Board attorney or judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone conferences expedite resolution, encourage cooperation, and sometimes obviate the need for a responsive brief; Board may require parties to contact case attorney prior to filing discovery motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial conferences for complex interlocutory issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If interlocutory questions have become so complex that resolution by correspondence or telephone is impractical and would be facilitated by an in‑person meeting, the Board may request that the parties meet in person at the Board's offices for a disclosure, discovery, or pre‑trial conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely utilized; Board has discretion to order in‑person conferences to resolve complex disputes when reasonable and not unduly burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability: identification of documents is not privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of discovery documents (as opposed to their substance) is not privileged or confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can be required to identify documents even if substance may be protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced compliance when full compliance unduly burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: If complete compliance with a particular request would be unduly burdensome, the Board may permit compliance by providing a representative sampling or some reduced amount sufficient to meet discovery needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board may allow sampling as an alternative where reasonable and responsive to needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer information: classes discoverable; names generally not
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of customers for involved goods/services are discoverable; names of customers (including dealers) generally constitute confidential information and are not discoverable, even under protective order. Exceptions: name of first customer and minimal number of customers in abandonment inquiries may be discoverable under protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between relevance (e.g., abandonment) and confidentiality; limited disclosures under protection are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and adoption of involved mark discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's selection and adoption of its involved mark is generally discoverable (particularly of a defendant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background on how and why a mark was adopted is relevant to TTAB issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: First use of mark is discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's first use of its involved mark is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-use facts are central to many TTAB disputes (priority, use in commerce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search reports discoverable; attorney comments privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: Search reports are discoverable, but the comments or opinions of attorneys relating thereto are privileged and not discoverable (unless privilege waived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce factual search reports but withhold privileged attorney mental impressions or analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial witness disclosure requirements (post‑Nov 1, 2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings commenced on or after Nov 1, 2007, a party is required in pretrial disclosures to name witnesses it expects will testify (or may testify), provide general identifying information (telephone number/address), and provide a general summary/list of subjects and documents expected to be introduced. If a party expects to call no witnesses, it must state so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witness identities and subject summaries are discoverable; parties need not disclose every exhibit they plan to introduce in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plans for expansion may be discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's plans for expansion may be discoverable under protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business plans and expansion intentions can be sensitive; they may be produced under confidentiality protections where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of third‑party use/registration discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's awareness of third‑party use and/or registration of the same or similar marks is discoverable to the extent the responding party has actual knowledge and the information is reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires disclosure of actual knowledge, not the results of an investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation history and settlements discoverable (limited detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning litigation and controversies including settlement and other contractual agreements involving the responding party's involved mark is discoverable; required details are names of parties, jurisdiction, proceeding number, outcome, and citation if published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full settlement documents may be discoverable though only minimal metadata is strictly required for legal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of non‑involved marks and goods
rubrics_metrics.description: A party need not provide discovery with respect to marks and goods/services not involved in the proceeding and having no relevance thereto; however, selling the same goods/services as the propounding party, even under a different mark, is relevant to likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope limited to relevance to issues in dispute; unrelated marks/lines typically not discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' names and addresses discoverable (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and addresses of a party's officers are discoverable; if there are many officers, provide names/addresses of those most knowledgeable of the involved activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target disclosure to officers with relevant knowledge rather than blanket production of all officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign use generally not discoverable (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's foreign use of its involved mark is usually irrelevant and not discoverable, except in cases such as alleged bad faith adoption to forestall foreign expansion or where a foreign mark is 'famous' in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign usage is context‑dependent; exceptions require showing relevance to the issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stockholders' identities generally not discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and addresses of stockholders or entities owned/controlled by a party are generally irrelevant and not discoverable unless there is an issue whether the parties are 'related companies' under Trademark Act §5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure limited to situations where corporate relationships are in dispute.
